TechnologyTab.title: Microsoft outage 'stark reminder' of how much we rely on tech
TechnologyTab.text:
A critical Microsoft outage lasting more than 22 hours has raised questions about how heavily vital services rely on a handful of major tech firms.

The disruption, which affected Microsoft 365 services such as Outlook, was caused by routine automated checks that took some servers offline, overloading the remaining ones with traffic.

The recovery took nearly a full day while engineers gradually restored services, highlighting how embedded the tech giant's services are in modern society.

Flora Hamilton, executive director of the Small Business Charter, said the outage was a "stark reminder" of how much firms "rely on digital systems" - like Microsoft Outlook - "to keep their operations running".

"For many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), access to email is fundamental to everything from communicating with customers and suppliers to generating income," she said.

The disruption was not just confined to businesses, but also affected organisations and public institutions around the world.

Around 430 million people globally use Microsoft 365, and issues were reported across more than 70 countries.

The fallout from the outage had a wide-ranging effect, knocking out email systems for the US House of Representatives and Australian intelligence agencies, as well as disrupting court systems in Singapore and airline support desks in India.

Microsoft has since apologised for the issue, which it said was due to a technical failure rather than a cyber-attack.

There was no "ETA" for when services will be fully recovered, Microsoft added in a statement late on Friday (GMT).

Walter Pasquarelli, an AI strategist, told the BBC that for governments, businesses and critical infrastructure, the outage had "put their vulnerabilities and dependence in plain sight".

"Looking ahead, as AI assistants are plugged into our email, calendars and files, a failure like this may spread even further," he said.

TechnologyTab.title: Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world
TechnologyTab.text:
At least 74 countries were affected by the Microsoft outage which was detected after midday US Eastern Time (17:00 GMT) on Thursday.

Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and artificial intelligence software Copilot, all experienced "connectivity problems", the company said.

As of early Friday afternoon (GMT), Microsoft was reporting improvements, with email queues "significantly reduced and approaching normal levels".

From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, the disruption was widespread. Here is what happened around the world.

In the US, staff with the House of Representatives told Politico, external their work had been halted by the outage.

"We all use Outlook, that's our life, everything is there, our calendar is there, our boss's calendar, so it has been a challenge … with no access to our Bible," one House staff member said. "There goes a day of legislative work."

Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic both reported problems.

OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which caused some tools not to work as expected.

Courts from Los Angeles to Texas also warned that communications might be delayed.

Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on 12 November, rescheduled to 16 November, citing business disruptions caused by the outage.

Meanwhile, officials in some US cities encouraged citizens to call local offices and agencies where needed instead of using email.

The City of Austin in Texas account posted on X early on Friday: "Due to an ongoing Microsoft Outlook outage, City of Austin employees cannot receive or send emails at this time.

"City phone lines remain operational, and 911 Emergency services are not impacted."

In Canada, a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto declared a "code grey", indicating an infrastructure failure.

The company, Unity Health Toronto, said its teams were having trouble sending or receiving email but that patient care was not affected.

Other hospitals, including Canada's largest children's hospital SickKids, also reported its staff having issues accessing phone calls and emails.

Via Rail, Canada's national train network, said in a post on X that its passengers might not be able to receive emails about their trips because of the outage.

Disruptions were also reported by Canadian municipalities, including the City of Ottawa and the City of Vancouver. Both urged residents in a notice to call in for any urgent issues.

In Japan, some companies reportedly turned to fax machines to maintain communications.

"Can't send emails because of a Microsoft outage, so we're switching to fax for the regular updates we usually send as PDFs. Analog is strong," one unnamed X user was quoted as saying by the Japan Times, external.

The Japanese government said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.

"We understand that Microsoft is working to restore services, and we will continue to monitor the company's response," Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki told reporters.

Singapore also confirmed the outage had affected some government systems, but stressed "emergency services remain fully operational".

Singapore's courts also said they were "experiencing issues with incoming and outgoing emails", urging people to contact them by telephone for urgent matters.

In the Philippines, the Supreme Court warned that "responses to emails and other transactions may be delayed".

In India, the outage was disrupting work for many on Friday, with emails not landing and Teams calls not going through smoothly.

People working in the equity markets told BBC News they had panicked when they realised they could not access daily research reports before their morning meeting where they make their big decisions of the day.

"Outlook wasn't working. We fortunately have an alternative so it was not a problem. But we conduct most of our calls, especially with big clients, on Teams - that has been a challenge," a senior executive with a big Indian brokerage said on condition of anonymity.

Firms in China use software that has been made locally - WPS Office is a favourite - but the Microsoft outage caused frustration there too.

Outlook is one of the few reliable channels for many offices and businesses in the country who work with colleagues across the world.

China operates one of the world's most sophisticated systems of internet censorship, known as the Great Firewall, which restricts access to many Western websites including Google, Facebook and Instagram along with many international news organisations including the BBC.

European stock market operator Euronext advised listed companies on Friday morning to use the phone to communicate corporate information because of the Outlook email disruption, Reuters reported.

Speaking to the same news agency, the head of Germany's BSI cybersecurity agency, Claudia Plattner, said the country's authorities had not been affected because they did not rely on Microsoft 365 services.

However, Reuters reported that Germany's national rail operator, Deutsche Bahn, was having difficulties sending out timetables for diverted trains due to the outage.

Plattner added the disruption was "affecting the whole world". "It is a global disruption that spans a vast number of data centres – stretching from Asia right across to the US, via Europe," she said.

In Antalya, Turkey, advisers and officials attending the UN Climate Change Conference, Cop31, were left frustrated by the outage.

James Young, a climate change adviser at the Inuit Circumpolar Council, the organisation which represents around 180,000 Inuit people living in the Arctic, told Reuters the council relied on emails and Microsoft Teams to communicate across several countries.

"It's just been really frustrating and challenging to maintain contact with our colleagues and to be able to effectively participate here," he said. "I think our dependence on technology leaves us vulnerable to situations like this."

In the UK, GPs, police and pharmacies were among services affected.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report.

Politicians are also affected. At Westminster, MPs were reporting their access via parliamentary accounts to Microsoft products was down.

A parliamentary spokesperson said: "We are aware of the global issue affecting Microsoft email services, which is impacting users of the parliamentary network. We are working with Microsoft to resolve the matter as quickly as possible.

"Alternative communication arrangements are in place, allowing today's business to continue."

Some parts of Asia, Europe and Africa were unaffected, according to Downdetector. These include Russia, where the use of Microsoft applications is heavily restricted, or phased out in favour of domestic alternatives.

However, this could also be a case of under-reporting in some countries, where Downdetector is among the websites blocked due to censorship.

One winemaker in South Africa said almost his entire business had been brought to a "standstill" by the Microsoft outage.

"It's incredibly frustrating," Peter Pentz added. "We export a lot, so communication with exporters in Europe has come to a standstill."

Order processing, dispatch, communications and even "critical production work" were halted, he said, as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations".

TechnologyTab.title: NHS, schools and police forces hit by Microsoft outage
TechnologyTab.text:
Key services across the UK, including the NHS, GPs and schools, have been affected by a global Microsoft outage.

Pharmacies and businesses have also been hit after email and messaging services went down.

NHS England said patients should still attend appointments unless told otherwise, while several large police forces are urging the public to call if they want to report a crime.

Microsoft said services were now gradually being restored globally after a problem caused by a higher-than-usual stress on its servers, but users could still experience disruption.

The government said it was working closely with the firm to assess any impact on its services, while local authorities warned that some council services were being affected.

The full extent of the impact of the outage - which is affecting Outlook, Teams and Copilot - and the time it will take to restore the systems remains unclear hours after users first reported issues.

Some 430 million people use the online tools worldwide.

The chief executive of the NHS Alliance, which represents the healthcare system in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, said the outage was affecting some services including emails.

NHS trusts in England were enacting measures to minimise disruption to critical services, a spokesperson said.

Patients have been told to continue to use 999 in an emergency and otherwise contact 111 by phone or online, or their local pharmacy.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains. Practices in Hampshire and Shropshire have told patients to phone them or come into the surgery if they have an urgent need.

A National Pharmacy Association spokesperson said the outage was affecting pharmacies' ability to communicate with GP practices and some patients, so "waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions".

The overall impact on health services remains unclear. Much of the NHS calendar is linked to diaries using the Microsoft system, but workflow practices differ between hospitals and trusts.

There are anecdotal reports of c-sections being cancelled and hospitals only accepting urgent referrals - though the impact on elective treatments has yet to be confirmed.

The GMB union's national secretary Rachel Harrison said the outage was having a "serious impact" on ambulance and NHS trusts.

"Those who work in 111 and 999 services are unable to refer patient details in the normal way which is creating a massive backlog and has the potential for chaos," she said, though "emergency and life-threatening call outs appear to be unaffected".

Meanwhile, police forces in England and Wales - including the Metropolitan Police, Greater Manchester Police and Police Scotland - have said online forms may be affected. They are urging people to call them about any time-critical by non-emergency matters.

Downing Street said it was looking to get a "full picture" of the the extent of the outage's effect on government services.

In England, the Local Government Association warned that some services may be disrupted but plans were in place to ensure people "continue to receive the support they need".

Because the outage affects key organisational and communication platforms that are integrated, many other workplaces have been affected.

That has included schools, where teachers, office staff and parents have all had to navigate being unable to access key resources on calendars, emails and internal cloud servers.

One head teacher at a primary school near Newcastle said safeguarding systems had also been affected, meaning staff were having to report concerns in person instead of logging them, while another in Cheshire said his had been forced to delay sending out termly school reports.

Universities have also suffered disruption to online systems, including tools used to submit assignments.

Some, like the University of Portsmouth and University of Aberdeen, have extended deadlines or waived late submission penalties.

Royal Mail said some of its online services were unavailable and email notifications about deliveries may be impacted, but post was still being collected and delivered as normal

MPs have been unable to access their parliamentary accounts. A spokesperson said alternative arrangements were in place

The Scottish government has activated its "resilience operations" as it assesses the impact of the outage

MSPs also confirmed that Holyrood's emails systems were down, meaning they were unable to communicate with constituents or access urgent casework

Some businesses are reverting to using paper or moving to different communication platforms like WhatsApp.

Some workplaces are reverting to using paper or moving to alternate communication platforms like WhatsApp to keep their businesses ticking over.

But others have been left struggling without the Microsoft tools.

Caroline Wade, who runs her own PR agency in Kent, told the BBC that the outage had caused her "huge disruption" as she was unable to send pitches and invoices.

Meanwhile, 29-year-old Georgia Young, from Staffordshire, was due to complete a house purchase today with her partner but said it had now been delayed.

"We've waited eight months to get to this point, it seem like it's out of reach again," she said.

Dave Walker said the outage was threatening his fledgling bakery and wine bar's online pre-Christmas sales, while Stirlingshire resident Lewis Bowles said he was unable to access his tickets for a Sunday rugby match.

EntertainmentTab.title: Noel Fielding 'appalled' by jokes he made with Russell Brand
EntertainmentTab.text:
Noel Fielding has said he is "appalled" by jokes he made alongside Russell Brand when the pair appeared together on TV and at live shows.

The Great British Bake Off presenter said in a statement to the Sun he was "horrified and deeply disturbed" to learn of Brand's crimes, after the disgraced comedian was jailed for rape and sexual assault.

Footage of Fielding and Brand joking about rape with TV presenter Jonathan Ross on an episode of Channel 4's Big Fat Quiz of the Year in 2007 has resurfaced in the aftermath of Brand's conviction.

Fielding described "some of the jokes" he made as "horrible and inappropriate", and said he had not been in contact with Brand "for many years".

"I was horrified and deeply disturbed to learn of Russell Brand's crimes, which I was completely unaware of until they became public knowledge. My thoughts are with the women whose courage brought him to justice," Fielding said.

"I appeared on TV, radio and live charity shows with him, and whilst we played it up for the cameras and in the media, I considered it a professional relationship, rather than a personal one. I have had no contact with him for many years.

"Looking back at some of the jokes I made alongside him I was appalled. They were horrible and inappropriate, and I very much regret them."

Ross has also released a statement distancing himself from the remarks, saying that his "thoughts are with the many, many women who have bravely come forward."

Among the resurfaced footage is a clip of Brand and Fielding laughing on an episode of The Russell Brand Show, which aired on BBC Radio 2 in 2007. In it, Brand joked about kissing and holding an underage grasshopper.

"How do you even know if it's a child or an adult? You don't even care, do you," Fielding responded.

Brand can be heard replying: "It's a mistake I've made. I've had a lot of problems in the past, because I thought a grasshopper was above age. Before I know it, I'm in it, right, I'm kissing it, I'm holding it. Then it turns around and looks at me with onyx eyes and says: 'I'm 12.'"

Brand and Fielding also performed charity gigs together as The Goth Detectives.

EntertainmentTab.title: Sotheby's auction of $180m Van Gogh challenged over claims it was 'sold under duress'
EntertainmentTab.text:
Auction house Sotheby's says it is working to resolve a dispute over the intended sale of a painting by Vincent van Gogh.

Châtaigniers en Fleurs, which carries an estimate of $180m (£136m), is due to go under the hammer in New York on Wednesday.

But representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family - earlier German owners of the work - say it may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

Sotheby's say its own "extensive research" has not established this, but say they will work with the family to try and reach a solution.

"Sotheby's takes provenance and restitution matters extremely seriously and has undertaken extensive research into the ownership history of Châtaigniers en fleurs," Sotheby's told the BBC in a statement.

"We are aware of the concerns recently raised by representatives of the Fischer heirs and have been in dialogue with them regarding the painting's history.

"While our research to date has not established that the painting was sold under duress, we recognize the importance of engaging thoughtfully and constructively with the family and are committed to working toward a mutually satisfactory resolution."

The painting - whose name translates as Blossoming Chestnut Trees - is being sold as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.

Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.

It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.

The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotherby's says.

Four other owners have had it since before it was put up for auction this year.

Fischer family heirs have instructed a lawyer who, according to the New York Times, external, has written to Sotherby's.

He is said to have told the auction house the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis.

The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.

EntertainmentTab.title: Eurovision Asia: Philippines wins continent's first song contest
EntertainmentTab.text:
The Philippines have won the very first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, hosted in Bangkok and with 11 countries vying for the title.

Nineteen-year-old singer Carmelle was always a front runner with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra, complete with its catchy rap section.

She earned 211 points in total - 93 from the jury and 118 from the public vote - ahead of Thailand's MANG x DAOU in second place with 170 points.

There was a joyous atmosphere at the One Bangkok Arena as the crowd cheered the contestants and celebrated the popular winner.

Carmelle, the youngest contestant in the competition, was an obvious favourite with the juries and the public despite strong showings from several nations.

Other notable acts included MANG x DAOU, whose emotive duet Aroma elicited huge cheers from the home crowd.

Bangladeshi beatboxers Beatmosphere eschewed the traditional backing track, instead using their voices to replicate the sounds of drums and basslines.

And Laos's Thinla performed her crowd-pleasing song Bae in a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit.

However, the Laotian song had a unintentional second outing after the music video was played over an apparent technical issue during the broadcast - meaning it was the last song the audience heard before the vote.

The voting system worked much the same as the European Eurovison, with the public vote accounting for 50% of the result and the other 50% coming from the 11 national juries - with additional points awarded from a rest of the world vote.

Here's how the final scoreboard ended:

1. The Philippines - 211 points

2. Thailand - 170 points

3. Vietnam - 164 points

4. Malaysia - 152 points

5. Laos - 139 points

6. Bhutan - 126 points

7. Republic of Korea - 113 points

8. Mongolia - 94 points

9. Nepal - 69 points

10. Cambodia - 61 points

11. Bangladesh - 35 points

Also performing during the broadcast was 2026 Eurovision Song Contest winner Dara from Bulgaria, who performed her winning song Bangaranga and new song Bad Idea.

Thai superstar Jeff Satur also made an appearance, hitting the high notes in his performance of Black Tie.

Eurovision in Asia was an idea that has been talked about for decades, but one that never seemed to materialise - despite many false starts - until now.

There is a huge enthusiasm here for Eurovision Asia, but a large number of the audience were established fans of the original contest from other countries and regions of the world.

Speaking after the show, fan Zelie Pereira - who travelled from Scotland to Thailand to attend - said she was "very happy" with Carmelle's win.

Korea, Vietnam and Laos also received praise from Pereira and her friends Michael Peters and Scarlett Massie, both from England.

"It was amazing, a very high standard," said Massie.

"The dance was amazing. The sets were amazing. The costumes were amazing. The singing was amazing. Incredible", Peters added.

They confidently declared that "Asia Vision" should be the name for next year's show.

For some, it seems the excitement for another edition is already building.

However the crowd at the One Bangkok Arena thinned out not long after the Philippines singer Carmelle lifted the trophy.

The arena was crowded, but not full, and it's still not clear how much commitment there is among regional broadcasters to keep the contest going and expand it to more than 11 countries.

EntertainmentTab.title: Owain Wyn Evans completes Children in Need bike ride in Cardiff
EntertainmentTab.text:
Presenter Owain Wyn Evans has completed his challenge of cycling through all four UK nations to raise money for BBC Children in Need.

The Welsh host of BBC Radio 2's Early Breakfast Show rode almost 400 miles, setting off from Glasgow and finishing in Cardiff on Friday.

The challenge started on 9 November in Scotland and over the next five days, Owain rode through Northern Ireland, England and Wales and raised £4,760,086 in the process.

Reflecting on his journey, he said: "This has been the hardest challenge of my life, 100%.

"I can't believe I'm here. It's overwhelming, all the love and passion and commitment people have shown."

In total, Children in Need raised £38.7 million in its 46th campaign.

The BBC said Owain's challenge would be the "greatest-ever distance" covered in a Radio 2 endeavour for the charity.

He crossed the finish line in Cardiff's Central Square just after 11:00 GMT, and was greeted by a crowd cheering him on before he was met by his husband, Arran Rees.

Owain, 42, whose bike was named Shania Chain, and decked out in Children in Need colours - Pudsey's favourite yellow with coloured spots - said: "Thank you so much everyone, from me and Shania.

"Honestly, this has felt so far away for such a long time. I can't believe that I'm here with this welcome and the sun's out."

Hollywood actor Luke Evans announced the route to Owain each day on BBC Radio 2.

During the 640km feat, he was also surprised with the premiere of Steps' brand-new version of their debut hit 5, 6, 7, 8, retitled 5, 6, 7, donate, which featured new lyrics and extra vocals.

It was recorded to help boost Owain's spirits on the longest day of his challenge.

EntertainmentTab.title: Police investigating David Walliams over reports alleging serious sexual offences
EntertainmentTab.text:
The Metropolitan Police has launched an investigation into David Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences".

It comes after ITV News and the Guardian published reports alleging that Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

The Met said that the allegations being investigated are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian, but as "part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences".

When those allegations were first reported, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

In a statement released on Friday, the Met said it had "received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s".

"Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers," the statement added.

Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney said: "We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offence to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened.

"We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process."

Allegations against the entertainer and children's author were published after he lost a legal bid to stop claims against him being made public by the media.

Some of the women in the investigation accused Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers.

One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.

He said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

The Guardian and ITV News said that several of the women, who do not know one another, allege they were targets of unwanted sexual advances from Walliams.

The investigation also claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another.

Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room.

In a letter addressed to journalists working on the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams wrote: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret.

"And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

Walliams shot to fame in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent and launched a best-selling series of children's books.

EntertainmentTab.title: Timothée Chalamet among Hollywood stars and charity heroes stepping up for BBC Children In Need
EntertainmentTab.text:
Timothée Chalamet and his Dune co-stars were seen pranking Rylan Clark during this year's Children in Need on Friday.

The Oscar-nominated actor was set up with behind-the-scenes suggestions in an Impractical Jokers-style set-up during an interview with Zendaya, Jason Momoa and Anya Taylor-Joy about the third instalment of the film franchise.

This year's Children in Need show also featured Radio 2 presenter Owain Wyn Evans and a "challenge squad" of young people completing feats in the name of charity.

The appeal raised almost £39 million to help children and young people across the UK.

The three-hour show was hosted live from Salford by Alex Jones, Mel Giedroyc, Rylan, Sara Cox and Tyler West.

They welcomed Wyn Evans, who has been the latest Radio 2 DJ to put himself through a gruelling challenge for Children In Need, following in the footsteps of the likes of Sara Cox and Paddy McGuinness.

Wyn Evans completed his 400-mile four-nation cycle ride through England, Scotland, Northern Ireland and his native Wales - finishing in Cardiff on Friday.

He raised more than £3.8m along the way.

EntertainmentTab.title: Rosalía scoops historic third best album award at Latin Grammys
EntertainmentTab.text:
Spanish star Rosalía has made history as the first woman to win the best album award at the Latin Grammys three times, after being recognised for her project Lux.

The singer took home five trophies in total, including two for her track La Perla which was named song of the year and best pop song.

La Perla was also nominated for record of the year but missed out to Argentine singer Milo J's song Niño.

Rosalía released Lux last year to rave reviews and collecting her award at the ceremony in Las Vegas on Thursday, she said: "To all the people who told me I wasn't good enough, or that my music was too weird, I'm thankful I didn't listen."

The Barcelona-born artist then added: "Now I'm winning these prizes."

Rosalía, who opened the ceremony with a performance of some of her biggest songs, was honoured with the prize for best alternative music album.

She also picked up best shortform music video for her track Sauvignon Blanc.

The singer had previously won best album for El Mal Querer in 2019 and Motomami in 2022 - and her third Lux is also tipped to be a favourite when nominations are announced for the Grammys next week.

It was also a big night for Puerto Rican reggaeton legend Daddy Yankee, who won the person of the year award.

He performed some of his best-loved tracks including Gasolina and Con Calma, and was joined on stage by rappers including LL Cool J and French Montana.

Punjabi singer Diljit Dosanjh, who collabed with Daddy Yankee on Pokito, even took a break from his Aura India tour for the set, making him the first Indian artist to perform at the Latin Grammys.

Dosanjh superfan Devanshi Arora described the singer's appearance as "a cultural revolution".

"It's really invigorating and motivating to see someone from my country has made it all around the world," she tells Newsbeat.

She sees a lot of similarities between South American and Punjabi communities and hopes this leads to more collaborations - with a link-up between Dosanjh and Bad Bunny top of her wishlist.

Daddy Yankee was presented with the lifetime achievement award by Janet Jackson, who told him in Spanish that his music "has inspired an entire generation".

EntertainmentTab.title: Guilty or redeemed? Our critics’ verdicts on this week’s UK cinema releases
EntertainmentTab.text:
In a sentence Screen adaptation of Suzie Miller’s international stage hit stars Cynthia Erivo as a lawyer whose career defending rape suspects is undermined by experience.

What our reviewer said “A blazingly fierce, effortlessly commanding central performance from Erivo, like something from classical drama, powers the movie.” Peter Bradshaw

Whispers in the Woods ★★★★☆

In a sentence Director Vincent Munier takes his father and son into the Vosges forest in France in an emotional study of human-animal interaction.

What our reviewer said “A subtle, tender work that evokes the need to pass on interest and engagement in the natural world to younger generations, but which manages to avoid feeling too preachy or sanctimonious.” Leslie Felperin

In a sentence David Wilkinson’s compassionate film deals with his own bowel cancer treatment, and asks why so many much younger people are getting the same diagnosis.

What our reviewer said “This is a sobering but very compassionate, humorous, generous film, and one that shows how Wilkinson’s highly personal and unselfconsciously confessional style has grown into something very watchable and distinctive.” Peter Bradshaw

A Fox Under a Pink Moon ★★★★☆

In a sentence Refugee Soraya Akhlaghi filmed her perilous flight from Iran and precarious new life over five years on her phone, reassembled here with boldly imaginative animations.

What our reviewer said “A born creator, Akhlaghi channels her struggles and despair into florid, intense drawings.” Phuong Le

In a sentence Story of the US army’s first Black special ops team at work in Vietnam, relating the incredible bravery they showed in the face of battle and unrelenting bigotry.

What our reviewer said “The title of course refers to the soul music that became anthemic to these soldiers, but also, with grim irony, to their sense that their souls had died in the jungle, fighting people they felt were just like them.” Peter Bradshaw

Give Me the Ball! ★★★★☆

In a sentence Sparky and engaging documentary about tennis ace Billie Jean King, who fought her whole career to ensure the women’s game got the respect it deserved.

What our reviewer said “King was a ferocious force in women’s tennis from the 60s onwards and a vehement but polite advocate for equal rights on prize money.” Peter Bradshaw

In a sentence Johnny Depp stars as the celebrated miser who finds redemption in a new version of the Dickens classic A Christmas Carol.

What our reviewer said “As Scrooge, Depp is in fact rather good; theatrically bad-tempered and petulant and, as with his Jack Sparrow, I suspect Depp’s comedy timing and sonorous British accent might have been learned from his old Fast Show comrade Paul Whitehouse.” Peter Bradshaw

Traces of Justice ★★★☆☆

In a sentence Forensic scientist Cui Daozhi, the “Chinese Sherlock Holmes”, is the real-life central figure of a cop thriller that ranges across 30 years of gripping cases.

What our reviewer said “The latest from Chen Sicheng, prime mover behind the hit Detective Chinatown franchise, offers a disarming mix of propaganda, copaganda and gripping narrative.” Mike McCahill

The Mosquito Bowl ★★★☆☆

In a sentence Peter Berg directs a handsomely made second world war drama about an American football game before the battle of Okinawa.

What our reviewer said “Berg has a knack for grace within visual cacophony and chaos; graphic sequences in battle and from the 1944 Christmas Eve pickup game at Guadalcanal that gives the film its name suggest, far more than its anvil-heavy dialogue, the connections between the gridiron and the battlefield.” Adrian Horton

In a sentence Kunsang Kyirong’s debut feature is an elliptical, elusive drama that follows Kunsel, an introverted woman, through Toronto’s tight-knit Tibetan community.

What our reviewer said “In the end, the film fades like a vapour trail in the sky, its mood of disorientation and dislocation perhaps a reflection of Kunsel’s state of mind.” Cath Clarke

In a sentence Cristian Mungiu won his second Palme d’Or with this disquieting child abuse drama starring Renate Reinsve and Sebastian Stan.

What our reviewer said “Ultimately, the film does not compellingly deliver a blazing truth about its various relationships – but neither does it intriguingly withhold any such truth from us.” Peter Bradshaw

How to Rob a Bank ★★☆☆☆

In a sentence Nicholas Hoult, Anna Sawai and Pete Davidson play Robin Hood in an anti-capitalist caper movie that attempts to mix social commentary with action.

What our reviewer said “For a film that’s supposed to enrage and excite and energise, it’s all strangely, boringly flat and with a runtime stretching past two hours, surprisingly sluggish too.” Benjamin Lee

Re-released this week

The Man Who Fell to Earth ★★★★★

In a sentence David Bowie plays an intergalactic visitor who becomes a successful tech entrepreneur in Nicolas Roeg’s 1976 sci-fi story.

What our reviewer said “There is an extraordinary sui generis central performance by David Bowie, whose unselfconscious gentleness and vulnerability now look very moving and bizarrely authentic in a way that they didn’t in 1976.” Peter Bradshaw

Female Perversions ★★★★★

In a sentence Tilda Swinton’s first US film, from 1996, in which she plays a lawyer who searches for erotic adventures in a rework of Madame Bovary.

What our reviewer said “It’s an amazingly unselfconscious performance which marked her out as quite unlike any other female lead, all but impossible to cast in boilerplate Hollywood cinema.” Peter Bradshaw

Marie Antoinette ★★★☆☆

In a sentence Sofia Coppola’s biopic of the French queen, combining dazzling visual tableaux and formal set pieces in strict period, with new wave chart hits from the 1970s and 80s.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘It’s an architect’s dream’: five beautiful eco buildings around the world
EntertainmentTab.text:
With construction accounting for more than a third of global emissions, sustainable architecture is central to the world meeting its climate targets. The following five creations from around the world exemplify how “green” buildings can also be beautiful.

Children’s Village, Tocantins, Brazil

In Tocantins, central Brazil, the Canuanã school is a boarding school whose pupils come from remote farming communities across the region. In 2017, architects gave the school’s 540 boarders two new “villages” of dormitories, one for girls and one for boys.

The buildings are made from locally sourced timber and earth bricks. A vast canopy shades the complex, and perforated brick walls let air pass through, so the bedrooms stay comfortable without air conditioning even when temperatures reach 45C. Under the roof, rooms open on to shady, landscaped courtyards and airy verandas.

David Mikhail, the co-founder of Mikhail Riches, a UK practice specialising in sustainable design, says: “It is absolutely fantastic. So beautiful. It does a lot with little resource, which is the essence of a sustainable approach.” He adds: “I love the economy of it, and the huge sense of place they managed to evoke through such elegant and limited means.”

The architects have said their biggest challenge was convincing pupils and teachers that earth, brick and timber could feel modern rather than old-fashioned. They managed to do so by listening to students through 10 days of workshops to understand what they wanted from the design.

The Arc, Bali, Indonesia

The Green school in Bali is surrounded by jungle and promotes sustainability through learning in a natural environment. Since it opened in 2008, it has been built almost entirely in bamboo. Its gymnasium, the Arc, was completed in 2021.

Inspired by a mammal’s ribcage, the Arc’s bamboo arches span a 760 sq metre sports court without a single column interrupting the floor space. The arches support an undulating canopy, and natural ventilation comes from breezes that flow in at the base, while warm air escapes through vents at the top.

Bamboo is a highly sustainable building material because of how quickly it can regrow; large varieties reach building strength in just three to six years. “It is so fast-growing and sequesters a lot of carbon dioxide very quickly, so using it for building is a bit of a no-brainer if you can make it work,” says Mikhail. “And not only have they made it work, they’ve done it absolutely beautifully.”

Sara Kulturhus, Skellefteå, Sweden

Skellefteå, a small city just south of the Arctic Circle, is surrounded by 480,000 hectares (1.2m acres) of forest, and features wooden schools, a wooden road bridge, even a wooden multistorey car park. In 2021 it added Sara Kulturhus, a 20-storey cultural centre and hotel that is one of the tallest timber buildings in the world. It houses two theatres, a museum, an art gallery, the city library and a hotel.

The building is made of glulam – layers of timber glued together – and cross-laminated timber, a kind of super-sized plywood. The hotel rooms arrived as prefabricated wooden pods and were stacked into place. Building in wood saved a year in construction time compared with steel and concrete, while the timber came from trees harvested within 40 miles of the site, and replacement trees have since been planted.

“It promotes a love affair with wood and timber, and the localism of that in an area like Sweden is fabulous,” Mikhail says. “The lovely thing about cross-laminated timber is that the trees you use to make the panels don’t have to be elderly specimen trees. They can be relatively fast-grown and sustainably farmed.”

The Forest, Hobart, Australia

When the University of Tasmania was planning the redevelopment of its main campus in central Hobart, the architects chose to adapt what was already there rather than demolish it and start again. Two early 20th-century brick warehouses and a heritage-listed glass dome were stitched together into a single campus of classrooms and study spaces, which opened in February 2026.

At its heart is the glass dome, built in 1997. It is filled with about 3,200 native plants, including various species of ferns, and has an integrated watering, misting and fogging system that recreates rainforest-like growing conditions.

“You could argue the most sustainable building is actually no building, and the second most sustainable building is a refurbished old building,” says Mikhail. “That’s what this is: they’re taking existing structures and breathing new life into them, reimagining what they could be.”

Rammed Earth House, Cranborne Chase, UK

On the site of a former brickworks in the Wiltshire countryside, this house has been built from the ground beneath it. Rammed earth, which has been used since the Neolithic period, is a building material made of soil that has been compacted layer by layer into thick walls. Here, clay-rich soil was dug up and mixed with rubble from demolished outbuildings and local limestone.

The earth is “unstabilised”, meaning no cement has been added, which makes this one of only a few UK buildings made that way. Unstabilised earth could, in principle, simply go back into the ground if the house were ever demolished.

Rammed earth’s thermal mass also evens out temperature and moisture indoors, which the architects say will matter more as the climate warms. “As a piece of architecture, I think it’s phenomenal,” says Mikhail. “It’s an architect’s dream, and I’m slightly envious of it, I’ll be honest.”

“It’s like a beautiful piece of jewellery, and it riffs on lots of really lovely sustainable ideas.”

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘It’s like the wild west’: how AI has rocked the literary world
EntertainmentTab.text:
The romance novelist Coral Hart got her break writing books for Mills & Boon, the publisher of bodice-ripper paperbacks. In 2012, she decided to dip her toe in self-publishing. She felt drawn to dark romance, a subgenre featuring twisted, toxic love stories that was taking off online but that publishers didn’t want to touch. Three years later, things were going well enough that she decided to self-publish full-time.

Kindle Unlimited, where Hart sells her books, rewards prolific writers: the algorithm favours those who can produce a new book at least once a month. Hart says she knows of authors who hire more than a dozen ghostwriters to keep pace. By herself, Hart can write 10,000 words a day, but AI could help her produce many more. Since 2025 she has written 370 novels under 21 pen names using AI, earning herself “high six figures”.

Like any Kindle Unlimited author, she is only paid per pages read: it would make no business sense for her to churn out books that readers quickly abandon. “A bad writer or a bad storyteller is not going to get a good book out of AI. You still need to understand craft. You still need to understand structure. You still need to know what a reader wants,” she tells me, speaking via videocall from her home in South Africa. “So, it’s not taking the human out of the equation. It’s taking the friction and the time and the business blocks out of the way.”

One study (awaiting peer review), led by Tuhin Chakrabarty of Stony Brook University, estimates that around one fifth of recently self-published books contain at least 25% AI-generated text. Hart now teaches courses on how to use AI to produce books. Unless disclosing the use of AI becomes a legal requirement, she advises other authors not to do so because of the public response.

“The minute someone discloses [AI use] they get death threats, they get called names, they’re ousted,” she says. Hart is one of her pen names. After she talked to the New York Times earlier this year she was doxed and faced death threats. “I think the anger and hate comes from a place of fear,” she says. In the literary world, many people fear the tech will undercut and replace them. “I think people are very afraid of AI, and people in publishing are delusional in thinking that it’s not going to overtake our industry, that their screaming on social media is going to stop it.”

But the anger comes from another place, too. If large language models can spit out books that people want to read, or produce a convincing pastiche of your favourite writer, that’s almost certainly because they were trained on established writers’ stolen work. Last year, a class action lawsuit involving around 500,000 titles won a $1.5bn settlement from the AI firm Anthropic for alleged use of the writers’ work without consent. Other similar lawsuits are ongoing. Many writers oppose AI for both moral and aesthetic reasons. One group of 70 prominent authors wrote an open letter calling on the big five publishers – Penguin Random House, Hachette, HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster and Macmillan – to promise that they will “never release books that were created by a machine”. The publishers did not promise.

So where do we go from here? Will big name writers win the argument for keeping AI out of literature, or will our bookshelves and e-readers soon be crammed full of AI-generated stories? And if a reader can’t distinguish human from machine writing, does it still matter?

One literary agent told me that when it comes to AI, the atmosphere in mainstream publishing is like “the wild west”. The technology is outpacing the industry’s capacity to reckon with what it means that authors can – and already are – using AI to write their books. “We’re at a time where it’s all very much in flux, and I don’t think anyone has good answers – but certainly everyone’s talking about it,” says Liz Gately, a New York-based book scout.

Instead, there has been a spate of cancelled high-profile book deals and accusations against writers. In March, Hachette withdrew the romance novel Shy Girl from publication over evidence the author Mia Ballard used AI. Ballard claimed to the New York Times that an editor she hired may have been responsible for inserting AI-generated text. This year’s winner of the Commonwealth short story prize, Jamir Nazir, was accused of using AI, after readers – struck by odd phrases such as “she had the kind of walking that turned benches into men” – ran the story through Pangram, a leading AI detection program. He denies it. Pangram subsequently tested other entrants and concluded that since 2025, four regional winners were likely to have used AI.

In July, agents representing the debut novelist Jerry Falade withdrew from an eye-popping $2m (£1.5m) book deal after he was accused of using AI. He denied using AI for anything other than research. And then, last month, the Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien’s novel was struck off the Goncourt Academy longlist, France’s most prestigious literary prize, after social media users ran his novel through AI detection software. He, too, denied using AI to write his novel, but did admit to plagiarism in some of his other writing, including a short story he wrote more than a decade ago. After conducting its own investigation, his publishers Boréal dropped him in late October.

Falade – who like everyone I contacted in relation to these scandals declined to speak to me on record – wrote an essay pointing out that writing by non-native speakers or in “culturally unfamiliar” English is more often treated with suspicion. He also suggests the accusations against him may be tinged with racism. “I haven’t seen this kind of investigative zeal directed at white authors accused of using AI …” he writes, “apparently that level of scrutiny is reserved for a Black boy from Nigeria.”

It is true that every writer at the centre of these AI scandals has been an author of colour. In May, the author Steven Rosenbaum – who is white – was found to have accidentally inserted fabricated quotes into his book The Future of Truth: How AI Reshapes Reality when he used AI, which he disclosed in the acknowledgements. He said he regretted the errors but added that it “serves as a warning about the risks of AI-assisted research and verification”, which is why he wrote the book. His book wasn’t withdrawn.

One big problem is that when writers are accused, it is hard for them to clear their names. There is no definitive proof either way. Literary agents and book scouts are professional readers and say most AI-generated submissions (and these days they receive many) are very easy to spot. But, clearly, human judgment isn’t flawless, and evidence suggests that non-native and neurodivergent writers are more likely to raise false suspicion. Academic research estimates that Pangram is at least 95% accurate at detecting AI-generated writing, and it has near-0% rate of false positives – suggesting it is extremely unlikely that the tech would falsely label human-generated writing as AI.

Hannah Bowman, chair of the Association of American Literary Agents’ (AALA) AI special committee, says there’s disagreement on the way forward: some agents think AI detection software should be used routinely, others advocate for relying on relationships of trust. “I think it’s a shame that all of these things are getting addressed so publicly,” she says, with many scandals starting when journalists or social media users run work through AI detectors. “I worry for authors when they don’t have a chance to make a case in defence of their work … there needs to be a fair and thoughtful process, where if publishers and agents have concerns, they can discuss them with the authors.”

In the meantime, Gately, the book scout, says many agents have started recommending their writers don’t send documents as PDFs and save multiple drafts of their work (rather than resaving the same document) in case they are subject to AI accusations. The pervasive anxiety among agents and writers manifests in strange ways. One agent told me they were shocked to receive a manuscript from a writer they had worked with for many years – and who professed to hate AI – that used suspiciously “bizarre” words. She contacted the writer, who was “horrified”: the problem wasn’t that she’d used AI; it was that she was terrified of being accused of doing so and her efforts to make her prose sound “non-AI” had backfired badly.

Another unresolved question is if and when publishers should withdraw books. If Falade’s book was good enough to impress multiple publishers and attract an astonishingly high, multimillion-dollar advance, does it matter how it was written? (Falade, incidentally, has recently signed with a new agent.)

Thad McIllroy, a publishing expert and author of The AI Book Revolution, says he was surprised when Shy Girl was cancelled. The cancellation was partly his fault. After being alerted to online rumours that the book was written using AI, he decided to run it through Pangram, and then approached the New York Times. “I felt so stupid when [Hachette] cancelled it because it never occurred to me that that would have been the response,” he tells me. He anticipated that the publishers would either clean up the text or issue a disclosure on how AI was used. Shy Girl started out as a highly successful self-published novel, and the AI rumours started before Hachette acquired the manuscript. Once bought, the publishers edited the text considerably. McIllroy says he therefore finds it hard to believe that no one raised AI-concerns internally. Plus, he says, it’s a “really powerful book” that clearly resonated with readers, so why drop it the moment the story hit the media?

Both AI enthusiasts and haters say there’s an urgent need for more guidance from publishers, who hold the purse strings and are therefore the kingmakers in the books’ world. McIllroy says publishers need to be “brave” and publish extensive AI policies, outlining how they use the technology in-house and what authors are and aren’t allowed to do. He wonders if publishing houses aren’t doing this because they are in denial about AI, or if they are worried about alienating their highest-earning writers, who are almost all vehemently opposed to the tech. Tess Callero, a literary agent with Europa Content who describes the prospect of AI-generated fiction as “scary”, says she thinks publishers are biding their time because they want to keep the door open for AI. “If the big five publishers were coming down and saying we will not accept [AI-generated writing] it would be taken more seriously,” she says. “But they’re not, and you have to wonder the reason they aren’t. Is it because they see a future in which potentially these books could be monetised?”

One issue is US copyright law, which specifies that a book must be “human authored” and considers AI-generated text public domain. “Which is why it’s so problematic for publishers – because if it’s AI, they have no protection, they can’t have exclusive rights,” says Natalie Lakosil, a literary agent and chair of the copyright committee at the AALA. US copyright law protects AI-assisted work, but if the text has been produced by a machine it risks legal challenge (even if the copyright office, which asks for little detail, accepts the registration). It seems likely, Lakosil says, that this principle will be challenged in the courts eventually, but she is doubtful that the “human authored” requirement will be substantially changed. “The purpose of copyright protection is to protect human creation, to protect artists, and AI is not an artist,” she says. That said, she does believe the law needs to find ways to accommodate writers who want to experiment creatively with AI. She says publishing is in the midst of a “freakout period” comparable to the advent of e-books, which didn’t kill the market – as many feared – but did permanently change it.

In 2023, Stephen Marche wrote the crime novella, Death of an Author, using three AI programs – it is, to anyone’s knowledge, the first AI-novel to be reviewed by the New York Times. It could only be released as an audiobook, because of copyright concerns. Marche has been experimenting with AI in his fiction since the early 2020s. “Publishing has both become incredibly moralistic and at the same time it keeps getting rocked by these scandals,” he tells me. “The people like me who are very conscious about its use, and who both understand the technology and its limits and are not using it in a cheap way, in a cheating way, we’re totally excluded. But you know the scammers will find a way.” He says he would love to see an “experimental blossoming of creative forms” using AI, as is already happening in the art world.

The way forward, Marche says, is full transparency: there is a “very clear moral line” in labelling what is and isn’t AI generated, just as we currently distinguish between fiction and nonfiction. Even those who hate the idea of AI writing (myself included) might recognise that on rare occasions it can be powerful, precisely when it is not trying to pass as human. In Vauhini Vara’s moving essay Ghosts, for example, she uses generative AI to express things she cannot bring herself to write about her sister’s death. The piece is a conversation between a human and a machine that explores the expressive limits, and possibilities, of both kinds of language.

Most likely, AI-generated books will enter mainstream publishing in some form, and will introduce more slop into the market. But Marche points out that our culture is already awash with dull, derivative stuff. He recently went to see a Hollywood action movie that was so formulaic that although it was not made with AI it may as well have been. “There’s this garbage out there that’s worthless, some of it is AI generated, some of it’s human generated. You’re trying to make meaningful shit in this context and how do you do that? Some of it’s going to be made by people. Some of it with AI,” he says.

In France, a new prize – the Prix Pascal de Littérature IA – was launched last month for fiction writers who are working with AI. It seems probable that some AI-assisted books will be good enough that discerning readers cannot necessarily tell that a human has not written them. A recent study, also led by Chakrabarty of Stony Brook University and awaiting peer review, found that in blind experiments, when expert readers (students on leading MFA writing programmes) compared passages written by their MFA colleagues and those written by AI models trained on established writers, and then fine-tuned, they tended to prefer the AI generated text. Would they still prefer the texts if they knew they were AI? Maybe some people will be happy to read such books, although even the most beautiful AI-generated text is a Frankenstein monster, borrowed feelings and observations about the human condition stitched together by an algorithm that has no human qualities, no capacity to love or to feel. But probably many readers would choose human writing. Every agent I spoke to felt committed to protecting the human. “We’re in the human creativity business, not in the business of giving robots jobs,” says Doug Wallace, managing director at Andrew Nurnberg Associates International, a network of literary agencies. AI is “not going to be a big problem because we won’t let it become a big problem”.

EntertainmentTab.title: James Blunt: ‘Do I have a nickname? Yes, it rhymes with blunt’
EntertainmentTab.text:
You were a punching bag for such a long time after You’re Beautiful became a massive hit but your consistent good humour is deeply admirable. Does it ever get tiring?

It was a surprise, at the beginning. I was just a little guy with a dream. And when you achieve your dream, you think people would be happy for you. For them not to be happy for you but angry with you, for your song, seems irrational, an overreaction. It is interesting how people generally want to tear people down for achieving their little dreams. But I’d had a real proper job before that [as a captain in the British army]. My friends might have been on operations in Afghanistan or Iraq, so if I were to complain to them at the time saying, “Oh, the Guardian said something really horrid about me and gave me three stars for my album” – they would be able to talk about who had lost their lives or limbs that day, and that put it all in perspective. And perspective is everything.

Then you start thinking really clearly. A journalist might say, “Hey, I read something negative about you online” – I can either start defending that or put it in perspective, which is: I’ve just played a concert to 15,000 people and those 15,000 people spent really hard-earned money to buy a ticket and booked hotels or flights to get there and queued up and, if it’s in England, queued in the rain. So am I really going to get upset by one negative tweet when 15,000 people really invested themselves in me? It’s all about perspective.

What is the best thing about owning two pubs?

The beer in my life is always free.

Are you very good at pulling a pint?

The staff in my pubs, because of who I am and the shame they sometimes feel, try to keep me out back doing the dishes rather than front of house. I understand why. It is how we roll.

Ed Sheeran and Carrie Fisher are the godparents of your children. What wisdom did you hope each of them would impart?

I hoped Carrie would look after herself. That’s why I asked her to be a godmother – I could see a destructive human being and I wanted her to care enough for herself that my son might know her. And it wasn’t to be.

And Ed and I had a very similar journey. We were singer-songwriters inspired by similar musicians, found ourselves managed by the same management, found ourselves signed to the same record label – but he just did it better. If you’re going to have your child be inspired by someone, point them in the direction of someone who does it better than you.

I understand you love a rave. How often do you get to one?

Not as much as I’d like, to be honest. I live in Ibiza and my favourite nightclub is a club called Pacha, which opened in 1973. When I was 13 years old, I was on a family holiday here and I walked past Pacha and told my friend, “I am going to live here, and I am going to go to that club.” The moment my first album, Back to Bedlam, became a hit, the first thing I did was buy a house in Ibiza, which is where I’m calling you from now. I later moved to Ibiza when I was a pariah in my own country and I wrote All the Lost Souls, a pretty dark and miserable second album. But the thing that kept me going was the dancefloor in Pacha … I wrote a song called 1973, the year Pacha opened. And then the DJ Pete Tong remixed it, so I would be in that club, listening to my own song, about the club that I was in – which is kind of mental.

There are other clubs I really love. Ushuaïa is like a Miami pool party and they’ll occasionally ask me to perform there. Sometimes I’ll drive down there, I park out the front, the security walk me to the stage and hand me a microphone, I’ll climb on to the stage, sing, crowd surf, go back on the stage, sing the final chorus, hand the microphone over, walk off the stage and drive home to put my kids to bed. That is either really rock’n’roll or really square, I am not sure which.

What is the best piece of advice you have ever received?

Don’t shit where you eat.

Who taught you that one?

Pretty much everyone I know.

What is the weirdest thing you have done for love?

Obviously I am a purveyor of saccharine songs, so I need to up my game when it comes to romance. So last Valentine’s Day, I hired a helicopter, flew over my house and threw 100,000 red rose petals at my wife in the garden below. I thought that was pretty good. She thought it was OK.

Who would you like to play you in the biopic about your life?

My mother really thought Tom Cruise but, if I’m totally honest, I know it’s more likely to be Alan Partridge.

What are you secretly really good at?

I do a really good gorilla impression. And! [James Blunt uses his brow to wiggle his scalp so it moves distinctly from his face] I actually have a wig that no one knows about. I don’t know anyone else can do that but I literally can move my whole scalp and hair as if it were a wig. It’s real. I haven’t managed to monetise it.

Do you have a nickname, and what is it?

Yes, it rhymes with blunt and it’s a tiny bit shorter. It’s character building!

Actually, it is bizarre that my name later became cockney rhyming slang for that. That’s one of my greatest achievements. I have a few things that I find genuinely an achievement – like I have a ski lift named after me in Switzerland, and a burger named after me. But to have cockney rhyming slang for your own name is amazing.

I have also heard about the James Blunt Museum, in a Herefordshire phone booth.

Yeah, a huge, huge deal for me as well. I have been known to go there just to give it a quick clean from time to time. It’s not too far, just a quick six-hour drive. I go there for the morning, clean it, head back home. It’s worth a visit if you find yourself in the northern hemisphere. I really recommend it.

Final question – you were just on Celebrity Traitors. If you could be on another reality show, what would it be?

I swore that I would never do a reality show. Ever. And I have lived and breathed by that proclamation. My manager doesn’t even bring me those shows. But my wife signed me up to this without telling me. And I really wish she hadn’t.

EntertainmentTab.title: Masterpieces haunted by brutal past could send records tumbling at Sotheby’s
EntertainmentTab.text:
Twelve rarely seen masterpieces glowing with life and beauty will go on sale at Sotheby’s in New York on Wednesday.

The collection, which resembles a miniature Courtauld gallery, includes Van Gogh’s towering chestnut tree, Monet’s shimmering vista of the Tuileries and Paul Cézanne’s Arlequin, a portrait of his son in a red and black diamond-patterned costume whose angularity pushes into abstraction and must have inspired Picasso’s Harlequins.

Sotheby’s has titled its auction Legendary because the Blaquier-Arrieta collection from which these canvases come is regarded as so tasteful and high class. The paintings, acquired by a wealthy Argentinian couple mostly in the 1970s, are what you would expect to see in a museum, not their Buenos Aires apartment as old photos show. What a shame they are stained by allegations of abduction and murder.

The Blaquier-Arrieta collection was funded by sugar, but this is not about the history of sugar and enslavement in the Americas. Carlos Pedro Blaquier, the head of the Ledesma sugar company, was suspected of being involved in the “disappearance” of hundreds of people in the Jujuy region one July night in 1976, known as the Night of the Blackout. The local electricity, which was under Ledesma’s control, cut out, allowing arrests to be made in darkness. Witnesses described people being carried off in Ledesma’s company vans. Survivors testify they were held and tortured on the company’s premises.

It was one of the many atrocities carried out across Argentina between 1976 and 1983 by the military dictatorship. On the Night of the Blackout, according to the European Center for Constitutional and Human Rights, most of the approximately 400 people seized were trade unionists who worked for Blaquier’s Ledesma sugar company. Up to 55 are still missing, presumed murdered.

Blaquier was 85 when charges were finally brought against him in 2012, long after the dictatorship’s fall. He was accused of “being the main participant in 29 cases of unlawful detention”. But it never went to trial because legal appeals delayed proceedings until his death in 2023 aged 95.

But this is about beauty, right? Well, beauty and money. It is predicted that Van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs and Cézanne’s Arlequin may sell for record prices for both artists: the Van Gogh was estimated “in the region of $180m” (£136m), Sotheby’s said. That would soundly beat the record for one of his works, which is $117m. Could it really make that, given it is not one of his most famous paintings?

The answer is quite possibly. This captivatingly melancholic masterpiece depicts a voluptuous, flowing, windswept street in Auvers-sur-Oise, where he moved to in 1890 after leaving the asylum. But when you look harder, everything is slightly unbalanced and out of kilter, from the yellow road and deep blue sky to the immense tree that dwarfs people below it. A storm is coming. He would shoot himself a couple of months after finishing this painting.

A Van Gogh no longer has to be one of his most famous to sell for megabucks. He is so universally idolised that even his socks would sell for millions - and Châtaigniers en Fleurs really is ravishing.

The blood spilt in the Night of the Blackout haunts this sale. Sotheby’s ignores the troubling side of the story in its publicity material, despite it all being in the public domain.

“We are of course aware of the reports concerning Carlos Pedro Blaquier,” said a Sotheby’s spokesperson. “He was never actually convicted of a crime; in fact, he maintained his innocence throughout, stating he had no knowledge that his company’s resources were being used to facilitate illegal activity. Naturally, we defer to the courts and the legal process on matters like this … we do not believe they detract from the quality or significance of the artworks themselves.”

And so this auction will write the “legend” of the Blaquier-Arrieta collection into the history books, while the alleged crimes of Blaquier and the Ledesma sugar company slip into footnotes. This is about visibility. I can see the bright reds, blues, greens and yellows in André Derain’s fauvist masterpiece Boats at the Port of Collioure (Lot 2). But I can’t see the up to 55 people taken away that night in 1976 who have never been found. They are gone, disappeared. Let the bidding commence.

GeneralTab.title: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
GeneralTab.text:
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

The US has not confirmed Zelensky's comments, and a US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties".

The Ukrainian leader's comments came after US envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky as part of US efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others while Russia has said another Nato member on its border is unacceptable.

Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. It controls most of the industrial region of Donbas and Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine is unwilling to give up sovereign territory.

"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.

He went on to say that if he received a specific proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.

Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted. It has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.

Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.

Other Nato members apart from the US are wary of membership for Ukraine - and it is understood that Ukraine itself sees that as unrealistic.

The Kremlin has always been fiercely opposed, too. It is one reason why Russia started this war in the first place.

It is possible the American envoys were exploring Ukraine's "red lines" when it comes to occupied land in the Donbas. Zelensky said recently that the US mediators believed Kyiv only had to cede territory to achieve peace and were applying pressure, keen to do a deal as soon as possible.

Ukraine is sure that Russia's ambitions are far greater and has long seen Nato as its only sure protection.

So it is also possible that Zelensky made this suggestion public in order to re-open a discussion that had been considered all but closed.

He maintains that the idea is now "back on the agenda" as part of an "extremely difficult conversation" on European security.

It also looks like Ukrainian push-back against Russia's renewed hardline stance. Moscow now talks about a "new European security architecture", which is long-standing Russian code for a weaker Nato.

The issue appears to have been the main focus at the latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi this week.

Hours after Zelensky's remarks, Jared Kushner appeared keen to dampen down any US offer of Nato membership for Ukraine, urging "confidentiality" in a sensitive process.

He said that "maximalist" proposals had been reported from the negotiations, along with "strong political rhetoric".

In what read like a reproach to Kyiv, Kushner referred to "private discussions" aimed at exploring new ideas about ending what he called a "horrible war".

He said the hope was that those ideas might lead to new proposals or breakthroughs.

Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.

It has insisted again that it will not agree to a ceasefire until a final peace deal is in place that would include Ukraine ceding control of those parts of the Donbas Russian troops have not captured, in addition to the Crimean peninsula Moscow annexed illegally in 2014.

The latest round of talks come after a period of fraught relations between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities deep inside Russia, which Trump had asked Ukraine to pause to facilitate the supply of Russian diesel to ease global fuel prices.

Zelensky then accused US officials of limiting Ukraine's Starlink internet service, which it uses to co-ordinate defensive operations, while Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" and called for fresh elections.

Elections are suspended while Ukraine remains under martial law, but Zelensky has previously said he was willing to hold them within months of a peace deal being reached and would give up the presidency in exchange for Nato membership.
